title: Strength and wisdom, given to the one who did good.
subtitle: Maturity as a gift, not just an age
then: Having told of his childhood, the story jumps to Musa as a grown man. Allah gave him {reward}judgement and knowledge{/reward}; Mujahid said this means prophethood. The verse ends with a rule: {idea}this is how Allah rewards those who do good{/idea}.
now: You are turning thirty, or forty, and expected to suddenly be wise. Birthdays do not do that. {idea}Clear judgement grows out of how you have been living{/idea}: the honest choices, the kindness no one saw.
old: Wisdom will come to me as I get older.
new: Allah gives judgement and knowledge as a reward for doing good, not just for getting older.
try: Do one good thing today purely for Allah and tell no one about it.

title: One blow in anger, and a man was dead.
subtitle: How fast a fight can go too far
then: Musa entered the city at a time when people were not paying attention. Two men were fighting, one from his people and one from Fir'awn's. When asked for help, he struck the other man with his fist and {trap}the man died{/trap}. Musa immediately named it {idea}Shaytan's doing{/idea}.
now: Someone insults your brother in the car park and you step in hot. A shove becomes something worse. {trap}Taking a side in a fight you do not understand{/trap} can wreck lives in seconds. Musa did not defend it; he called it what it was.
old: If I was defending my side, what I did was justified.
new: Anger in a moment of loyalty can still be Shaytan's work, and I should say so plainly.
try: Next time you feel heat rising in an argument, step back one pace and breathe before you act.

title: I wronged myself, so forgive me. And He did.
subtitle: The fastest way back after a terrible mistake

row.title: explaining myself
sub: it was not really my fault

then: Right after the blow, Musa turned to Allah: {idea}"My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me."{/idea} No blaming the fight or the other man. {reward}Then He forgave him.{/reward}
now: You snapped at your mother and slammed the door. Your mind starts building the case for why you were right. {idea}Musa's words are shorter: I did wrong, forgive me.{/idea} Allah answers that kind of honesty.
old: What I did is too serious to be forgiven.
new: Owning my wrong and asking Allah plainly is the door, and He is quick to open it.
try: Tonight, name one wrong to Allah in your own words, with no excuse attached, and ask forgiveness.

title: Never again will I back the wrongdoers.
subtitle: Turning forgiveness into a promise
then: Ibn Kathir explains the favor as {reward}the prestige, power and blessings{/reward} Allah had given Musa. Because of that, Musa vowed he would {idea}never again be a helper of the criminals{/idea}, those who go against Allah's commands.
now: Your skills, your login access, your influence in the group chat. They can be lent to someone else's wrong without you noticing. {idea}Forgiveness is the moment to decide whose side your gifts are on.{/idea}
old: My abilities are mine to use however people ask.
new: Every favor Allah gave me is a reason never to put it at the service of wrong.
try: Think of one thing you are good at. Decide one thing you will never use it for.

title: The same man, the same fight, the next day.
subtitle: When someone keeps pulling you into trouble
then: Musa spent the day {trap}afraid, watching for the consequences{/trap}. Then the same man who had asked for help was fighting another Copt and called him again. Musa told him plainly: {idea}you are clearly misleading{/idea}.
now: The cousin who always has a new fight and always needs you to back him. The friend whose drama you keep getting dragged into. {idea}Sometimes the kind thing is to name the pattern{/idea}, not to jump in again.
old: If someone on my side calls for help, I have to answer.
new: Loyalty does not mean following someone into the same trouble every day.
try: Think of one person who keeps pulling you into conflict. Decide calmly what you will say next time.

title: A frightened man blurted out the secret.
subtitle: How a hidden mistake came to light
then: Musa moved toward the Copt, but the Israelite, {trap}out of cowardice and weakness{/trap}, thought Musa meant to hit him. He cried out about yesterday's killing. Only the two of them had known. The Copt carried the news to Fir'awn, who {trap}resolved to kill Musa{/trap}.
now: You covered for a friend once, and now in a panic they throw your name into the room. {idea}Fear makes people say things they never meant to.{/idea} Be careful whose secrets you share, and how you act when you are scared.
old: The people I helped will always protect me.
new: Fear can turn anyone careless, so I should guard my own conduct before relying on others.
try: Next time you feel cornered, say nothing for ten seconds before you speak.

title: One man ran across the city to warn him.
subtitle: The courage to take a different route
then: Fir'awn's chiefs were {trap}taking counsel together to kill Musa{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says this person is called a man because {idea}he had the courage to take a different route{/idea}, shorter than the pursuers, and reached Musa first with sincere advice.
now: You overhear the plan in the office to blame someone for a failure. You could say nothing. {idea}Or you could be the person who runs ahead{/idea} and quietly warns them. That takes courage, not power.
old: If I overhear something unfair, it is safer to stay out of it.
new: Sincere advice, given at risk, can be the turning point of someone else's life.
try: If you know something a friend needs to hear for their good, tell them kindly today.

title: Alone, afraid, and praying while he walked.
subtitle: Leaving everything with one short dua
then: Musa left Egypt on his own. Ibn Kathir notes {trap}he was not used to being alone{/trap}; he had lived in luxury and leadership. He walked out fearful, watching behind him, and asked {idea}"My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people."{/idea}
now: You leave a job, a marriage, a home, and drive away with everything in the back seat. Your hands are shaking. {idea}You do not have to feel brave to pray.{/idea} Fear and dua can sit in the same breath.
old: If I am this afraid, my faith must be weak.
new: Even a prophet walked away afraid; the point is to turn to Allah while afraid.
try: Memorise Musa's short dua and say it the next time you walk into something scary.

title: No map, just hope that his Lord would guide him.
subtitle: Setting out without knowing the way
then: Turning toward Madyan, Musa said {idea}"Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the sound way."{/idea} Ibn Kathir says Allah did exactly that: He guided him to the straight path in this world and the Hereafter, and made him {reward}guided and a guide for others{/reward}.
now: First day in a new country. The bus map makes no sense, the language is strange, and you are not sure the move was right. {idea}Hope in Allah's guidance is a way to start walking{/idea}, even before the road is clear.
old: I cannot start until I know exactly where this leads.
new: I can set out with hope that my Lord will guide me as I go.
try: Before your next uncertain step, say: perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way.

title: Tired and hunted, he still noticed two women waiting.
subtitle: Seeing the people pushed to the side

row.title: my own problems
sub: I am the one in trouble

then: Musa reached the well of Madyan. Shepherds were watering their flocks while two women {trap}held their sheep back{/trap} so no harm would come to them. Ibn Kathir says {idea}he felt sorry for them and took pity{/idea}, and asked what was wrong.
now: You are stressed, broke, and exhausted, in the supermarket queue. An elderly man is struggling with his bags behind everyone. {idea}Musa had far more reason to look away{/idea}, and he still asked.
old: When my own life is falling apart, I have nothing to give.
new: Even at my lowest, I can notice the person being pushed aside and ask if they are okay.
try: Today, notice one person waiting at the edge of a crowd and offer help.

title: He helped, then sat in the shade and asked.
subtitle: The dua of someone with nothing left
then: Musa watered the flocks for the women, then went back to the shade. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and As-Suddi said he sat beneath a tree. There, with no home and no food, he said: {reward}"My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me."{/reward}
now: You helped your neighbour move, and you go home to an empty fridge and a rent reminder. {idea}You did not ask them for anything. Ask Allah instead.{/idea} Admitting you are in need is not weakness; it is the dua.
old: I should not ask Allah for small things like food or work.
new: Telling Allah plainly that I need any good He sends is exactly what Musa did.
try: Sit somewhere quiet today and tell Allah, in your own words, one thing you need.

title: The answer came walking shyly, with an invitation.
subtitle: Dua answered, and the fear finally lifted
then: When the sisters returned early, their father asked why, and sent one to call Musa. Umar described her as walking shyly, covering herself. Ibn Kathir notes {idea}her good manners{/idea}: she framed it as her father's invitation. Musa told his story and the old man said {reward}"Fear not. You have escaped."{/reward}
now: You prayed under the tree, and the reply comes as a text from someone you barely know: come by, my dad wants to thank you. {reward}Answers often arrive through ordinary people.{/reward} And sometimes the best answer is just someone saying you are safe now.
old: My dua was too small for Allah to answer so quickly.
new: Allah can answer a dua within the hour, through a person I never expected.
try: Look back at today and find one small thing that might have been an answer to a dua.

title: Hire the strong one who can be trusted.
subtitle: Two qualities worth looking for
then: One daughter told her father to hire Musa. Asked how she knew, she said {reward}he lifted a rock that only ten men could lift{/reward}, and on the walk he asked her to walk behind him and guide him. Ibn Mas'ud counted her among the three people with the sharpest discernment.
now: You are choosing a business partner, a flatmate, someone to marry. The talented one and the kind one are not always the same person. {idea}Look for both: able to do the job, and safe to trust.{/idea}
old: Skill is what matters when choosing someone to work with.
new: The best person to rely on has strength and trustworthiness together.
try: Ask yourself honestly which of the two, strength or trust, you need to grow in. Do one thing for it.

title: An offer of marriage, made without pressure.
subtitle: Eight years, or ten if you choose
then: The old man offered Musa marriage to one of his daughters if he tended the flocks for eight years, with two more {reward}as a favor, if he wished{/reward}. He added {idea}"I do not wish to put you in difficulty."{/idea} Musa was a fugitive with nothing; the father did not exploit that.
now: You are hiring someone desperate for work, or renting a room to a student far from home. You could push the terms. {idea}This father chose fairness and ease{/idea} with a man who had no bargaining power.
old: When someone needs me more than I need them, I can set the terms.
new: Dealing fairly and without pressure with someone vulnerable is what the righteous do.
try: In your next deal or request, make one part easier for the other person than it has to be.

title: Agreed, and Allah is witness to our word.
subtitle: A promise kept, and kept generously
then: Musa agreed and put the deal under {idea}Allah as witness{/idea}. Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Abbas, recorded by Al-Bukhari, that Musa {reward}fulfilled the longer and better term{/reward}, for when a Messenger of Allah said he would do a thing, he did it.
now: The contract says forty hours; the handshake said you would see the project through. {reward}Musa did the extra, not because he had to.{/reward} Treat your word as something Allah is watching over.
old: Once I have met the minimum, I have done my part.
new: With Allah as witness to my word, I can keep promises fully and even generously.
try: Pick one promise you made recently and finish it a little better than you said you would.
